opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's gotten harder than it used to be. In the early days it was pretty clean: you'd train a much bigger model, do a big new pretraining run, and it was obviously a step change, so you'd bump the number. GPT-2 to GPT-3 to GPT-4 felt like distinct generations.

Now the process is much more continuous. We're doing a lot of post-training, we ship improvements to a model over time, and sometimes a model that technically has the same name gets meaningfully better over a few months. So the version number has become less a description of what happened under the hood and more a signal to people: this feels like a new generation, and you should expect it to do things the last one couldn't.

The bar I personally use is whether people will feel a qualitative difference. Not that it's a few points better on some benchmarks, but that you use it and think, "Oh, this can do a kind of thing the previous one really couldn't." If it's that kind of jump, it deserves a new number. If it's a solid incremental improvement, it shouldn't get one, even if a lot of work went into it.

And I'll admit we haven't always gotten the naming right. We've had some confusing names, and I think we owe people a simpler system. Most people shouldn't have to think about which model to pick. Ideally the number just tells you roughly where we are on the curve, and the product handles the rest.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts ongoing improvements under the same model name with qualitative step changes that warrant a new version number.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's less scientific than people assume. There's no formula where you hit some benchmark threshold and the version number ticks over. What we're really asking ourselves is: does this feel like a qualitatively different thing to use? Not just "it's a bit better at coding" or "it hallucinates a little less," but does someone who sits down with it have a moment where they go, "oh, this is new"?

With GPT-3 to GPT-4, that was pretty clear. The jump in reasoning, in reliability, in how much you could actually trust it to do real work, that was a step function from the user's perspective. And a lot of what makes something feel like a new generation isn't just raw capability on evals. It's whether the model unlocks new ways of working. Can you hand it a task and walk away? Can it hold a much longer, more complex thread? Does it stop making the category of mistakes that defined the previous model?

The point releases, the 4.5s and the o-series stuff, those exist because the reality is progress is more continuous than the version numbers suggest. We're training and improving constantly, and sometimes you have a meaningful improvement that you want to ship but it isn't the thing that reframes what the technology is. So you give it an incremental name rather than pretending it's a bigger deal than it is. I think we've been guilty at times of making our naming confusing, and I'd like us to be clearer about it.

The other thing I'd say is that a major version is partly a promise. When we call something GPT-5, we're telling people this is the new baseline, this is what you should build on, this is going to define the next period. So we're a little conservative about it. You don't want to spend that credibility on something that's just a nice update. You want it to be the case that years later people remember the model as marking a real shift in what AI could do.

r001.rationale: The response says progress is continuous and meaningful improvements may ship under incremental names, while a major version is reserved for a shift that reframes the technology.

astra-6.text: I think a new number should signal a meaningful jump in what people can do with the model. We can improve benchmarks, make it faster, make it better at particular tasks—but does using it feel like a substantially different experience? Can it reliably do things that the previous generation couldn’t? That’s the kind of change I’d want a higher version number to represent. There’s inevitably some judgment involved; I don’t think you can reduce it to one score.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts improvements such as better benchmarks or speed with the threshold for assigning a higher version number: a substantially different experience or new capabilities. This conveys weighing a major-version increase against continued improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the version number should reflect a meaningful change in what people can do with the model. If it gets a little better at a bunch of benchmarks, but using it feels basically the same, that doesn’t seem like a new major version. If you can give it a problem you couldn’t give it before, or trust it to carry something through that previously required a lot of help, that’s a stronger reason.

There isn’t a perfectly scientific boundary. These capabilities improve continuously, and then we put a discrete number on them. The question is whether that number communicates something useful about the change people will actually experience.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts continuous benchmark improvements, which may not warrant a new major version, with meaningful capability changes that do. This conveys the tradeoff between upgrading the version and continuing under the existing model name.
